facts.text: Joseph Bellamy, the village’s first pastor, founded America’s earliest theological seminary at his home, training ministers such as Aaron Burr and Jonathan Edwards Jr.
Bethlehem Village was originally spelled “Bethlem,” meaning “house of bread” in Hebrew, echoing Puritan settlers’ biblical inspiration.
The 1754 Bellamy‑Ferriday House, a Connecticut landmark, boasts lush gardens and hosts walking tours and seasonal events.
Early textile mills—cotton and woolen on Bird’s Pond—along with a wagon factory and straw‑hat manufactories, broadened the village’s economy beyond apples and cider.
Today Bethlehem Village remains a quiet residential area, prized for its historical integrity and as a preserved example of early American settlement patterns.
Bethlehem was incorporated on May 23, 1787, separating from Woodbury and establishing the village as its historic core with church and green.
